0.title: The Truth About Sin
0.essay:
“Sin” sounds like an old-fashioned word. Yet it names something everyone has met: in the news, in their families and, if they are honest, in the mirror.

The most obvious doctrine

G. K. Chesterton once remarked that original sin is the one part of Christian teaching that can really be proved. No one has to teach a toddler to snatch a toy. Every generation hopes that better education, better laws or better technology will at last make better people, and every generation is disappointed. The Bible’s verdict is short and matches what we see: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).

The most resisted doctrine

And yet no doctrine is fought harder. We are happy to talk about mistakes, weaknesses, wounds and bad choices. We are much less happy to say that we have wronged God and deserve his judgment. A woman who came to a church course said it plainly: “I don’t mind being told I’m broken. I mind being told I’m guilty.”

Why the diagnosis is good news

A doctor who will not name your illness cannot treat it. If the human problem is only ignorance, we need a teacher; if it is only pain, we need a therapist. If it is sin, we need a Saviour, and God has given one. The Bible never shows us our sin to leave us in despair. It shows us the wound so that we will let the Physician near. The more clearly we see how deep sin goes, the more astonishing the grace that goes deeper still.

The chapters

What Sin Is; Where Sin Came From and How Far It Reaches; Two Ways to Run from God; What Sin Does; What God Did About Sin; and Living as Forgiven Sinners. For the practical battle against particular sins, see the study Fighting Sin & Temptation.

For reflection

What do you think of when you hear the word “sin”? Why do you think people find it easier to call themselves broken than guilty?

1.title: What Sin Is
1.essay:
Most people think of sin as breaking rules. The Bible says that, and much more. At its root, sin is a matter of the heart: loving something else in the place that belongs to God.

The Bible’s words

Scripture uses a cluster of words for sin, and each shows a different side of it. The commonest Hebrew and Greek words mean missing the mark, like an arrow that falls short of the target: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Another word is transgression, stepping over a line that has been clearly drawn. Iniquity means something twisted or bent out of shape. John adds that “sin is lawlessness” (1 John 3:4): not just a slip, but living as though no one has the right to tell us what to do. And the prophets often call it rebellion, the word used of a subject rising against a rightful king.

Together these words describe not accidents but people who see the line and step over it, because something in us does not want God to be God.

Against God first

After his adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband, David prayed, “Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight” (Psalm 51:4). That can sound strange. Had he not sinned terribly against Bathsheba and Uriah? Of course he had. But David saw that every wrong done to a neighbour is first a wrong done to the God who made that neighbour and gave the command.

That is why the Bible measures sin by God, not by our neighbours. Jesus said the great and first commandment is, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37). If that is the first commandment, then the first and greatest sin is not murder or theft. It is failing to love God with everything we are. Every other sin flows from it.

Good things made ultimate

Paul traces the human story like this: “although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him … and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images” (Romans 1:21–23). At bottom, sin is an exchange. We take the place in our hearts that belongs to God and give it to something he made.

Usually the idol is not a bad thing. It is a good thing turned into an ultimate thing: a career, a family, a relationship, money, comfort, a cause, even our own goodness. We look to it for what only God can give: worth, security, meaning, love that will not fail. Jeremiah puts it unforgettably: “my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13). Sin is not only wicked; it is foolish. We leave a spring for a leaking tank, and then wonder why we are thirsty.

Augustine described sin as disordered love. The things we love are often good; the trouble is the order. When we love anything more than God, even something lovely, our loves are out of order. You can tell what your heart worships by asking what you cannot bear to lose.

What we do, and what we leave undone

Sin is not only doing wrong. It is also failing to do right. “So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin” (James 4:17). The priest and the Levite in Jesus’ parable did nothing to the wounded man; they simply walked past (Luke 10:31–32). Many of us would pass a test on the first. Few of us would pass on the second.

Thoughts, words and deeds

In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus took the commandments inward. “You have heard that it was said … ‘You shall not murder’ … But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:21–22). And “everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). God’s law reaches past the hands to the heart. Contempt is murder in seed form; lust is adultery in seed form. No one who has listened to Jesus can say, “I have kept the commandments.”

The thing she could not lose

A mother of three would never have called herself a sinner in any serious sense. She was kind, generous and faithful. Then her eldest son left university and drifted, and she found herself sleepless, furious and controlling. A friend gently asked, “Is it possible you’ve needed his success to know you were a good mother?” She was silent for a long time. Her children had become the place she looked for worth. It was the first time sin made sense to her: not a list of crimes, but a love in the wrong place.

For reflection

Which of the Bible’s words for sin (missing the mark, transgression, iniquity, lawlessness, rebellion) best describes your own experience? Why does David say his sin was against God “only”? What good thing in your life is most likely to become an ultimate thing? Which sins of omission are you most prone to?

2.title: Where Sin Came From and How Far It Reaches
2.essay:
If sin is so universal, where did it come from? And how deep does it go? The Bible’s answers are humbling, but they are also strangely freeing, because they tell the truth about us.

Not from God

Sin is not part of the way God made the world. Everything he made was “very good” (Genesis 1:31). Sin came in when our first parents listened to the serpent, doubted God’s goodness and reached for what he had forbidden. The study Creation & the Fall tells that story in detail. Here it is enough to say that the fall was a real event in history, and that it is also every person’s story: we too have doubted God’s word and wanted to be our own gods.

God is sovereign over all things, including the fall, yet he is never the author of sin. “God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one” (James 1:13). Sin is the creature’s act, not the Creator’s. Scripture holds both truths, and so must we. We cannot blame God for our sin, and we need not fear that evil has slipped out of his hands.

In Adam

Paul writes, “sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned” (Romans 5:12). Notice the last words: “all sinned”. Paul means that when Adam sinned, the whole human race sinned in him. He stood as our representative, as a head of state signs a treaty for a whole nation. “By the one man’s disobedience the many were made sinners” (Romans 5:19).

Christians have understood this in different ways. Pelagius, in the fifth century, taught that Adam only set a bad example which we copy; each of us starts with a clean slate. The Eastern Orthodox churches teach that we inherit from Adam mortality and a corrupted nature, but not his guilt.

This commentary’s view: with Augustine, the Reformers and the historic Reformed confessions, all sinned in Adam. His guilt is counted to the whole race, and all are born both guilty and corrupt. David confessed, “in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psalm 51:5), and Paul says we were “by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind” (Ephesians 2:3). This can feel unfair. But notice where Paul is going. The same principle by which Adam’s sin is counted to us is the principle by which Christ’s righteousness is counted to believers: “so by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). If we refuse to be represented by Adam, we have no ground to be represented by Christ. The doctrine that humbles us is the doctrine that saves us.

From the inside out

Jesus located the problem precisely: “from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, foolishness” (Mark 7:21–22). We like to think evil comes mainly from outside: bad upbringing, bad company, bad systems. Those things are real, and they shape us. But Jesus says the spring is inside. And the heart cannot be trusted to judge itself: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?” (Jeremiah 17:9).

Total, not utter

Reformed Christians call this total depravity. It does not mean that people are as bad as they could be. Unbelievers can be honest, brave, loving and wise, and God’s common grace restrains evil in every society. It means that sin has reached every part of us: mind, will, feelings, desires, body. There is no untouched room in the house from which we can begin the repairs. The study The Doctrines of Grace (in its chapter Total Depravity) sets out the texts in full.

Free, and bound

Are we free, then? In one sense, yes. No one forces our choices; we do what we want. But that is just the problem. “Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin” (John 8:34). We are free to follow our desires, but we are not free to change them. The will follows what the heart loves, and the fallen heart does not love God. That is why we need not advice but new birth.

No one has to teach them

A primary school teacher, not a churchgoer, once said that thirty years in the classroom had settled one question for her. “I’ve never had to teach a single child to lie,” she said. “I’ve spent my whole career teaching them not to.” She loved her pupils, but she had watched the same patterns appear, unprompted, in every class: grabbing, blaming, excluding, showing off. Without knowing it, she had described original sin.

And here is the wonder. God knew all this about us before he set his love on us. Nothing in us surprised him, and nothing will. The gospel is not that God loves the nice version of us we show the world. It is that “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

For reflection

Why does it matter that God is not the author of sin? How does Romans 5:19 connect Adam and Christ? Where have you seen Jeremiah 17:9 at work in the way you judge yourself? In what sense is your will free, and in what sense is it bound?

3.title: Two Ways to Run from God
3.essay:
There are two ways to run from God. One is to break all the rules. The other is to keep them all. The first is easy to recognise. The second is sin’s subtlest disguise.

Two sons

Luke 15 opens with a complaint. “The tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, ‘This man receives sinners and eats with them’” (Luke 15:1–2). Jesus answers with three parables, and the last is about a father and two sons.

The younger son asks for his share of the inheritance while his father is still alive, which amounts to wishing him dead. He goes to “a far country” and squanders it “in reckless living” (Luke 15:13). That is the first way to run from God: lawlessness. Take the gifts, ignore the Giver, live as you please.

The elder son never leaves home. He works hard and keeps every rule. But when his brother comes back and the father throws a feast, “he was angry and refused to go in” (Luke 15:28). Listen to what he says: “Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat” (Luke 15:29). He has been obeying, but not out of love. Like his brother, he wanted the father’s goods; he simply used a different method. At the end of the story it is the younger son who is inside at the feast, and the elder son who is outside, in the dark, refusing to come in.

Lost at home

That is the shock of the parable. You can be lost in a far country, and you can be lost at home. You can run from God through immorality, and you can run from him through morality. Both sons wanted the father’s things rather than the father. Both wanted to be in control: one by breaking the rules, the other by keeping them so well that the father would owe him.

The elder brother’s sin is harder to see because it looks like goodness. It shows itself in anger when grace is given to the undeserving, in a cold joylessness about duty, in contempt for those who fail, and in the feeling that God has not treated us as well as we deserve. Both sons had put themselves at the centre.

Two men in the temple

Luke 18 tells a parable “to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt” (Luke 18:9). The Pharisee’s prayer is full of true statements. He really does fast and tithe. Yet his prayer is a mirror, not a window. He mentions God once and himself constantly. His thanksgiving is really comparison: “God, I thank you that I am not like other men” (Luke 18:11). The study Humility & Pride looks at this parable as a lesson in humility. Here notice what it shows about sin: his very goodness had become his saviour. He was trusting in his record, not in God’s mercy.

The tax collector brought no record, only a plea: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). He went home justified. The Pharisee, for all his virtue, did not.

Pride at the root

Underneath both forms lies pride: the refusal to receive from God as a beggar. The irreligious person says, “I will run my own life.” The self-righteous person says, “I will earn my own standing.” Luther described the sinful heart as curved in on itself, turned inward so that it uses everything, even God and religion, for its own ends. Paul had been the perfect elder brother: “as to righteousness under the law, blameless” (Philippians 3:6). Then he met Christ, and he counted it all as loss, wanting to “be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ” (Philippians 3:9).

So the gospel is not religion. Religion says, “I obey, therefore God accepts me.” The gospel says, “God accepts me in Christ, therefore I obey.” And the parable leaves a gap that only Jesus fills. A true elder brother would have gone out to the far country to look for his lost brother, whatever it cost. That is exactly what the Son of God did. He was perfectly obedient out of love, never to earn the Father’s favour but because he delighted in him, and he left his Father’s house to bring us home, at the cost of his life.

The elder brother in the pew

A long-serving church officer was asked to welcome a new member: a man recently out of prison, newly converted and visibly overjoyed. The officer smiled and shook hands, but on the way home he found himself seething. “Thirty years I’ve served this church,” he thought, “and no one has ever cried with joy over me.” That night it dawned on him that he was standing outside the party. He prayed the tax collector’s prayer, perhaps for the first time with his whole heart.

For reflection

Which son are you more like by temperament, and how does that son’s sin show itself in you? Why is self-righteousness harder to repent of than open rebellion? Read Luke 15:28–32: what does the father’s going out to the elder son tell you about God? How is Jesus the true elder brother?

4.title: What Sin Does
4.essay:
Sin is never a private matter, and it never stands still. It damages our standing before God, our sense of ourselves, our relationships and the world itself. Seeing that clearly is painful, but it is the only way to see why the cross was necessary.

Guilt and shame

Sin brings guilt. Guilt is not first a feeling but a fact: a broken law and a just penalty owed, whether we feel it or not.

Sin also brings shame. When Adam and Eve sinned, they hid, and Adam said, “I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself” (Genesis 3:10). Guilt says, “I have done wrong.” Shame says, “I am wrong”: exposed, unworthy, unfit to be seen. Many people today feel little guilt but much shame, and cover it with achievement and image. The gospel answers both. Christ bears our guilt, and he also covers our shame and welcomes us.

Slavery

Sin promises freedom and delivers bondage. Habits become chains. Jesus said, “everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin” (John 8:34). We think we are choosing freely, until we try to stop.

Alienation

Sin separates. Most deeply it separates us from God: “your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God” (Isaiah 59:2). Then it separates us from ourselves: we become strangers to our own hearts, unable to rest. It separates us from one another: Adam blamed Eve within minutes of the first sin, and Cain killed Abel within a generation. And it disrupts our relationship with creation: the ground was cursed, work became toil, and the whole creation now groans (Romans 8:22).

Death and judgment

“For the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). Wages are what we have earned. And death is not the end: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27).

Jesus himself spoke often, and soberly, about hell. Christians have held different views. Most, through the centuries, have held that hell is conscious and unending. Some evangelicals, including John Stott (tentatively), have argued that the lost are finally destroyed rather than punished for ever.

This commentary’s view: hell is conscious, eternal punishment. Jesus sets the two destinies side by side in a single sentence: “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). The same word describes both, and we have no warrant to shorten one and not the other. This is not a doctrine to state with relish, and the Bible’s images (fire, darkness, exclusion from God’s presence) are meant to warn, not to entertain. At its heart hell is getting what sin has always wanted: life without God. God takes no pleasure in it: “Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23).

Not all sins are equal

Every sin deserves God’s judgment, but not every sin is equally serious. Jesus told Pilate, “he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin” (John 19:11). He said that the servant who knew his master’s will and ignored it would be punished more severely than one who did not know (Luke 12:47–48). Sins against greater light, sins that harm the vulnerable, sins planned and repeated, are worse than sins of weakness or ignorance. So God’s judgment will be perfectly fair, and we should not flatten everything into “we’re all sinners” in a way that excuses abusers or crushes the tender-hearted.

The sin that will not be forgiven

Jesus also spoke of one sin that “never has forgiveness” (Mark 3:29): blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The religious leaders had watched Jesus drive out demons by the Spirit of God and declared that he had an unclean spirit (Mark 3:30). They were calling the clearest light darkness, with settled hostility.

So the unforgivable sin is not a single careless word, a dark thought, a moral fall or even a long backsliding. It is a final, hardened rejection of Christ. It is unforgivable not because Christ’s blood is too weak, but because the person refuses the only forgiveness there is. And here is the comfort: if you are afraid you have committed it, you have not. The hardened do not tremble. Your very fear shows that the Spirit is still at work in you. Notice how the passage begins: “all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter” (Mark 3:28). That is the wide door. Walk through it.

The thoughts she could not stop

A university student was tormented by horrible thoughts about the Holy Spirit that flashed into her mind uninvited, especially when she prayed. She became convinced she had committed the unforgivable sin. Her pastor explained that unwanted, hated thoughts are not settled rejection; they were the opposite of what she wanted. He also urged her to see her doctor, since intrusive thoughts like these are a recognised feature of anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder, and treatment is no failure of faith. With patient help, and the promise of Mark 3:28, she slowly found peace.

For reflection

Do you struggle more with guilt or with shame? Where have you seen sin separate people from one another? Why does it matter that some sins are more serious than others? If you have ever feared the unforgivable sin, what does Mark 3:28 say to you?

5.title: What God Did About Sin
5.essay:
If you want to know how serious sin is, do not look first at the news, or even at your own heart. Look at the cross. There sin is seen at its worst, and grace at its greatest.

Sin at its worst

At Calvary every form of sin we have met in this study gathered in one place. Religious leaders handed over an innocent man out of envy; a governor sacrificed justice to keep his job; friends ran away. When God came among us in person, full of grace and truth, we killed him.

But the deepest thing happening at the cross was not what people did to Jesus. It was what God was doing through him. “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned, every one, to his own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

The cup

In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). In the prophets the cup is the cup of God’s wrath against sin. He was facing something no martyr has faced: the judgment of God on the sins of his people. On the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34). The Son, who had known the Father’s love from all eternity, entered the darkness that sin deserves.

In our place

The New Testament describes the cross in many ways. It is a sacrifice for sin, a ransom that frees slaves, a victory over the powers of evil (Colossians 2:15), and the supreme example of self-giving love. All of these are true. But at the heart of them all is substitution: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). “He was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5). “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Some Christians have placed the moral example of the cross at the centre, or the victory over evil, and some have said that the cross cleanses sin but does not turn away God’s wrath. Each sees something real.

This commentary’s view: at the heart of the cross Christ bore the punishment our sins deserved, in our place, turning God’s wrath away. The example and the victory flow from that. Paul says God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25), a sacrifice that turns away wrath. This is not an angry Father punishing an unwilling Son. The Father gave the Son, and the Son gave himself, in one shared act of love. The Judge took the sentence himself. The study The Person & Work of Christ sets this out more fully.

Just, and the justifier

Why could God not simply forgive? Because he is just, and because sin is real. A judge who waved away every crime would not be kind; he would be corrupt. The cross shows God’s righteousness “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). Sin is not overlooked. It is paid for. So forgiveness is free to us, but it was not cheap to God.

Every real forgiveness costs something. If someone wrecks your car and you forgive them, you do not make the damage vanish. You absorb it yourself. At the cross God absorbed the cost of our sin himself. That is why the gospel never makes sin small. It makes grace enormous.

Everything sin did, undone

Look back at what sin does, and see what Christ has done. Our guilt: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). God declares the believing sinner righteous, because Christ’s righteousness is counted as his. Our shame: Christ “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2), so that we could be welcomed without hiding. Our slavery: “our old self was crucified with him … so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin” (Romans 6:6). Our alienation: we are reconciled and adopted. Death: Christ rose, and death has lost its sting. Sin’s guilt is gone, its power broken.

Grace abounding

Paul gives a sentence to remember for a lifetime: “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). However high sin has risen in your life, grace rises higher. However deep the stain, the blood of Christ goes deeper.

The father who paid

A teenage boy borrowed his father’s car without asking and wrote it off. No one was hurt. He waited at home for the explosion. Instead his father sat down with him and said, “I forgive you.” Years later, the son learned that his father had been underinsured and had quietly worked extra shifts for two years to replace the car. “I thought I’d been let off,” he said. “I hadn’t been let off. He paid.” Forgiveness that costs the forgiver everything is the only kind that can bear the weight of a human life.

For reflection

What does the cross show you about the seriousness of sin? Why could God not simply overlook it? Which of sin’s effects most needs the answer of the cross in your life right now? Read Romans 5:20 slowly. Is there a sin you have thought too great for grace?

6.title: Living as Forgiven Sinners
6.essay:
Christians are not people who have stopped sinning. They are forgiven sinners, learning to live in the light: honest about sin, quick to confess, free from condemnation, and longing for the day when sin will be gone for ever.

Still sinners

Conversion breaks sin’s reign, but not yet its presence. John writes to believers, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:8–9). Paul, an apostle, cried out, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:24–25). This commentary reads Romans 7:14–25 as the honest struggle of Paul the believer, answered by Romans 8; the study Fighting Sin & Temptation explains that reading and gives practical help for the daily battle. A Christian who says, “I am still a sinner,” is not admitting that the gospel failed; he is telling the truth it taught him.

The godliest people usually feel their sin most keenly. Isaiah saw the Lord and cried, “Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). The closer you come to the light, the more dust you see.

Repentance as a way of life

Repentance is not only the door into the Christian life; it is the air we breathe there. To repent is to turn from our idols to the living God, and from our own righteousness to Christ’s. Elder brothers must also repent of good works done to put God in their debt.

Confession is the practical form of repentance. David knew what it was to hide sin: “when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long” (Psalm 32:3). And he knew the relief of bringing it into the light: “I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity … and you forgave the iniquity of my sin” (Psalm 32:5). Confession is not paying for sin with misery. It is agreeing with God about it, and then believing him about the forgiveness.

Conviction or condemnation?

Not every voice that speaks to you about your sin is God’s. Jesus promised that the Holy Spirit would “convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment” (John 16:8). But Scripture also calls Satan “the accuser of our brothers … who accuses them day and night before our God” (Revelation 12:10).

The Spirit’s conviction is specific: it names a particular sin. Accusation is vague: “You are useless; you always fail.” Conviction leads you to Christ; accusation drives you into hiding. Conviction brings godly grief that “produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (2 Corinthians 7:10); accusation brings worldly grief that turns in on itself and leads to despair. Conviction ends when you confess and believe the promise; accusation never ends, because it wants your ruin. When the accuser speaks, answer him with Paul: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33).

If you find that guilt has become crushing and constant, so that you cannot sleep or function, or you begin to think life is not worth living, please speak to someone straight away: your doctor, a trusted friend or pastor, or, if you are in danger, emergency services or a crisis line. Depression can make every sin look unforgivable; that is the illness speaking, not God.

When others sin against us

The doctrine of sin is realistic about wrongs done to us too. Forgiving is not pretending nothing happened. In our hearts we let go of bitterness and leave justice to God (Romans 12:19); full restoration of the relationship waits for repentance. Where there has been abuse, safety comes first. Forgiveness never means staying in danger or keeping silent: get to safety, and report abuse to the police or the proper authorities (Romans 13:4). The study Forgiveness & Reconciliation treats these hard cases with care.

The night he lost his temper

A father shouted at his teenage daughter, saying things he regretted at once. Lying awake, he heard two voices. One said, “You’ve always been like this. You’ll ruin her. Call yourself a Christian?” The other was quieter: “You were harsh and unjust. Go to her, and come to me.” The second sent him to his knees and, in the morning, to his daughter’s door with a plain apology. He had learned the difference between the accuser and the Spirit.

No more sin

The story will not end with the struggle. Of the new creation John writes, “nothing unclean will ever enter it” (Revelation 21:27), and “No longer will there be anything accursed” (Revelation 22:3). One day we shall see Christ and “be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Never again will we wound those we love or hide from God. The one who began the good work will finish it (Philippians 1:6). And for ever the redeemed will marvel that the God against whom they sinned is the God who bore their sin, and made them his own.

For reflection

Why do mature Christians often feel their sin more, not less? How can you tell the Spirit’s conviction from the accuser’s condemnation? Is there a sin you need to confess today, to God or to someone you have wronged? How does the promise of a world without sin change the way you fight sin now?
